items.title: Rubric Judgments Lack Uncertainty: Conformal Weighting for LLM Evaluation
items.abstract: Rubric-based evaluation is widely used to assess large language model (LLM) outputs by decomposing quality into multiple criteria and assigning each a binary judgment from an LLM verifier. However, judgment certainty varies substantially across criteria. Existing methods uniformly aggregate these judgments into a final score, implicitly treating every criterion as equally certain and overlooking this heterogeneity. As a result, uncertain judgments remain incorporated into reward estimation without distinction, potentially yielding misleading training signals for downstream reinforcement learning (RL). To address this limitation, we propose Uncertainty-aware Rubric Weighting (URW), a training-free framework that quantifies criterion-level judgment uncertainty via conformal calibration. Specifically, URW elicits a soft uncertainty signal from a fixed pool of paraphrased judgment templates and converts it into a per-criterion weight using split-conformal $p$-values with provable coverage guarantees. Extensive experiments demonstrate that URW consistently improves pairwise preference accuracy and delivers stronger downstream RL alignment.

items.title: Scene Reconstruction Using Ubiquitous Wireless Signals via Diffusion Posterior Inference Over physics-Grounded Representations
items.abstract: Knowing the layout of the physical world matters for many applications, yet the sensors we rely on for it (e.g., cameras and LiDAR) can fail in darkness, in adverse weather, or behind walls. Wireless signals do not face these limitations: every link between a base station and a user is shaped by the buildings it passes, reflects from, or is blocked by, leaving information about the surrounding scene embedded in the wireless channel measured at the endpoints. However, mapping channel measurements to the environment is a severely ill-posed problem: a measurement records only the structures that interact with the transmitted electromagnetic waves along its propagation paths, and even these observations can often be explained by multiple plausible scenes. We therefore formulate wireless scene reconstruction as posterior inference and develop a hierarchical framework with two complementary stages to approach this problem. A wireless foundation model, pretrained to respect propagation physics, transforms each channel measurement into a representation of the scene structure that shaped the observation. A diffusion model then jointly integrates representations from multiple measurements to model and sample the posterior over building occupancy, with consensus over samples producing the final reconstruction. We demonstrate that the framework can accurately recover building footprints from wireless channel measurements alone and show that its performance depends critically on both design components: physics-grounded representations expose scene-relevant information, while joint posterior inference coherently integrates complementary observations.

items.title: Sci$Π$vot: Benchmarking Principal-Investigator Judgment at Pivotal Moments of Scientific AutoResearch Agents
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can keep scientific experiments running for months with little human supervision, but reliable autonomous research also requires scientific judgment. Evaluating scientific judgment is difficult because research decisions are open-ended and depend on project context. We construct Sci$Π$vot, a 248-case benchmark of scientific judgment based on human corrections. The benchmark draws on records from six months of research in which senior researchers ran LLM agents on 26 projects across six scientific fields and repeatedly intervened to correct the agents' research judgments. In each case, an agent chooses between the original LLM plan and the human-corrected alternative, using only the project record available before the correction as context. We compare LLM and human performance and examine the effects of reasoning effort, access to the project record, and reconsideration. At medium reasoning effort with the project record, models systematically prefer the original LLM plan over the human-corrected alternative. Four of five frontier models perform below chance on the selected cases. The highest accuracy in the project condition across the tested models and reasoning effort settings is 63.5%, compared with 73.4% for fresh researchers. At medium effort, every model achieves lower accuracy with the project record than without it, and reconsideration does not consistently improve overall accuracy. Even with a human-corrected alternative available, frontier models struggle with the selected research decisions, while Sci$Π$vot supports systematic evaluation of scientific judgment for LLM agents.

items.title: Scoping One Health Foresight Collaboration among EU Agencies
items.abstract: This working paper constitutes the first deliverable under the EFSA contract RTD/2023/OP/0011 – Lot 1 on Foresight on Demand in Science, Technology, Research and Innovation Policy, implemented within the framework of multi-agency foresight on One Health and authorised by the European Commission, DG Research & Innovation, G1 – Common R&I Strategy and Foresight Service. It examines the relevance of the One Health approach for a broad range of European institutions and agencies and argues that One Health has become an increasingly important framework for addressing the complex and interdependent challenges facing the European Union. These challenges include emerging infectious diseases, antimicrobial and antifungal resistance, environmental pollution, climate change, food insecurity, mental health pressures, and widening social inequalities, all of which cut across traditional sectoral and institutional boundaries. The report situates One Health within its broader conceptual and policy context. It shows that the approach has evolved from earlier biomedical understandings centred on zoonotic disease and veterinary-public health cooperation into a wider framework linking human, animal, plant, and environmental health. In line with the recommendations of the European Commission’s Group of Chief Scientific Advisors, the report adopts the OHHLEP definition of One Health as an integrated and unifying approach aimed at balancing and optimizing the health of humans, animals, plants, and ecosystems. At the same time, it underlines that important ambiguities remain concerning the interpretation, scope, and operationalisation of the concept, especially in the context of European governance. The report therefore not only maps One Health as a thematic field but also examines how it can serve as a practical basis for stronger coordination among EU agencies and institutions. A central finding is that One Health is already relevant to a wide constellation of EU bodies, even if this relevance is not always explicitly recognised or institutionally coordinated. The report highlights the roles of DG SANTE, DG ENV, DG CLIMA, DG AGRI, and the Joint Research Centre, as well as agencies such as EFSA, EMA, ECDC, EEA, ECHA, EUDA, EU-OSHA, Frontex, EIGE, and ETF. These actors contribute complementary expertise across food safety, infectious disease monitoring, environmental protection, chemical safety, medicines regulation, occupational health, social inequalities, and preparedness. The report notes that cooperation has already advanced through initiatives such as the ONE Conference, the cross-agency One Health task force, and joint work on zoonoses and antimicrobial resistance. However, it also finds that collaboration remains uneven, fragmented, and often dependent on issue-specific rather than strategic coordination. Existing efforts show strong potential, but the absence of a fully integrated governance architecture continues to limit the EU’s capacity to translate One Health into a genuinely shared and anticipatory policy framework. On this basis, the report develops a broad and integrated overview of the main scientific themes currently shaping the One Health agenda. These include infectious diseases and health security, veterinary medical products, antimicrobial and antifungal resistance, environmental and climate-related health risks, animal health and welfare, public health and disease prevention, sustainable food systems, inequalities and governance, digitalisation and health, and education and training. A major contribution of the report is that it expands the One Health agenda beyond its more established focus on zoonoses and AMR. It argues that issues such as chemical pollution, microplastics, PFAS, unsafe food systems, occupational health, illicit drugs, mental health, militarization, nuclear risks, and the health implications of geopolitical change must also be considered within a One Health framework because they arise from and reinforce the interdependence of environmental, animal, and human health. The report therefore presents One Health not as a narrow technical field, but as a broader framework for understanding and governing systemic and interacting risks. The report also emphasizes that the One Health perspective is closely aligned with broader EU strategic priorities. It shows that One Health contributes not only to public health protection, but also to goals related to sustainable prosperity, food security, preparedness, climate resilience, social fairness, and democratic legitimacy. In this sense, One Health is framed as a governance approach capable of linking prevention, resilience, and sustainability across domains that are too often treated separately. The report repeatedly stresses that challenges such as climate change, biodiversity loss, environmental degradation, food insecurity, and health inequalities cannot be addressed adequately through isolated policy responses. Rather, they require integrated surveillance, coordinated foresight, and stronger institutional mechanisms capable of connecting evidence, preparedness, and action across sectors and scales. A further important conclusion is that One Health must be treated as both a scientific and institutional innovation agenda. The report identifies the need for stronger inter- and transdisciplinary collaboration, improved data sharing, harmonised surveillance systems, and clearer coordination mechanisms at EU level. It supports the view that the European Union should adopt a more coherent One Health strategy, backed by adequate resources, shared infrastructures, and long-term political support. Education and training are also identified as crucial pillars. One Health concepts should be integrated into academic, professional, and public learning environments, while digital tools, artificial intelligence, and data systems should be developed in line with ethical, inclusive, and sustainable principles. At the same time, the report warns that digitalisation, if poorly governed, may reproduce inequalities, deepen data divides, and generate new environmental burdens. In its final section, the report moves from thematic mapping to strategic foresight. It identifies a series of emerging and cross-cutting areas that merit particular attention in future collaboration. These include cross-border health threats and joint preparedness, chemicals and environmental exposures, illicit drugs and their environmental and social dimensions, climate change and health inequalities, social determinants of health, mental health, digitalisation, and militarization. Across all these areas, the report underscores the need for strengthened multi-agency collaboration and more systematic data sharing. It argues that the EU already possesses many of the institutional building blocks required for a stronger One Health approach, but that these assets need to be connected more effectively through coordinated foresight, shared analytical tools, and common strategic priorities. Overall, the report presents One Health as a necessary and forward-looking framework for European governance. It shows that the health of people, animals, plants, and ecosystems is increasingly shaped by interconnected pressures that no single institution, sector, or Member State can manage alone. By embedding One Health more firmly in research agendas, legislative initiatives, surveillance systems, education, and inter-agency cooperation, the European Union can improve its capacity to anticipate and respond to multidimensional threats while also advancing sustainability, equity, and resilience. In this sense, One Health is not merely a conceptual lens, but a practical foundation for future European collaboration in science, regulation, and strategic policy development.

items.title: SCRIBE: Scalable Contextual Representations of Interpretable Brain-Grounded Semantics
items.abstract: Understanding how the human brain constructs meaning from real-world language remains a fundamental challenge, as semantics depend on context that varies in natural settings. To enable the study of real-world linguistic meaning in the brain, we introduce SCRIBE, a framework grounded in a neuroscience-informed semantic space that leverages an ensemble of open-source large language models to generate interpretable, word-level semantic representations of arbitrary text. In a behavioral study with 921 participants, we show that human semantic feature judgments vary systematically with context, and that SCRIBE captures these shifts, reaching 75-81% of the estimated human noise ceiling. Using brain activity recorded while participants listen to naturalistic stories, we further demonstrate that SCRIBE predicts neural responses in language-selective brain regions, significantly outperforming non-contextual semantic representations. Variance partitioning reveals that SCRIBE explains unique brain-predictive information beyond syntactic features, suggesting that its representations capture aspects of linguistic meaning not accounted for by the measured syntactic features. Together, these findings establish SCRIBE as a scalable and interpretable foundation for studying natural language semantics in the brain.

items.title: Securing Intelligent Edge Ecosystems
items.abstract: With the advent of Internet of Things technologies and intelligent edge computing systems, the surface of cyber-attacks has been increasingly growing, which results in the problem of network security in distributed systems. This chapter will provide a review of intelligent intrusion detection methods using AI for secure intelligent edge ecosystems in the IoT. The chapter will discuss how machine learning, deep learning, and federated learning models are used together with edge computing systems to increase detection accuracy, reduce the time needed for detection, and maintain scalability while preserving data privacy. Furthermore, the proposed framework takes into account explainable artificial intelligence, privacy-preserving learning, and deployment techniques to overcome problems related to limited resource constraints of edge devices. Also, this chapter explores present security issues, application scenarios, implementation issues, and future perspectives, such as zero trust architecture, collaborative edge intelligence, and autonomous cyber defense systems.

items.title: SEFRQO-Plus: a self-evolving query optimizer via large language models and retrieval-augmented generation
items.abstract: Abstract Query optimization is a crucial problem in database systems that has been studied for decades. Learned query optimizers (LQOs) can improve performance over time by incorporating feedback; however, they suffer from cold-start issues and often require retraining when workloads shift or schemas change. We initially proposed SEFRQO, a Self-Evolving Fine-tuned RAG-based Query Optimizer, which leverages fine-tuned LLMs to address these challenges and uses in-context learning to achieve continuous evolution. However, its system design relies on the assumption of repetitive query workloads, requires executing queries statically upon their first encounter (incurring extra overhead), and utilizes only partial feedback from the best historical records (insufficient feedback design). In this paper, we present SEFRQO-Plus, which resolves the above limitations. First, we design a feedback-oriented vector database with query structure-aware embeddings to support effective similarity search, and we incorporate multi-layered histories as references to enrich the feedback. Then, we enhance the prompt optimization workflow by utilizing multi-dimensional historical feedback to drive continuous self-evolution. Moreover, we provide formal theoretical proofs to validate the advantages of our customized query group relative policy optimization. Evaluations show that SEFRQO-Plus outperforms state-of-the-art LQOs, achieving reductions of 66.52% and 69.79% in query latency for the complete CEB and Stack workloads, respectively, compared to PostgreSQL. items.title: Selection of Outcomes and Measurement Methods in Clinical Trials for Digital Therapeutics: Qualitative Analysis
items.abstract: Abstract Background In recent years, the availability of digital therapeutic apps in medicine, digital therapeutics (DTx), has significantly increased. To evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of DTx, an increasing number of scientific studies have been conducted in this field. Several authors have pointed out that a standardized approach to DTx evaluation is relevant to improving the comparability of apps in the future. Currently, it is unclear how study authors proceed when selecting outcomes and measurement methods (O&M) for DTx studies. Objective The primary aim of this study was to investigate how study authors currently select O&M in DTx studies, specifically for applications delivered in the form of apps. The secondary objectives were to collect suggestions for improving the comparability of DTx apps and studies in the future and to examine whether core outcome sets (COS) could represent a possible solution for enhancing comparability. Methods This study was based on 19 semistructured interviews. All interview partners had prior experience in planning and conducting DTx studies. The interviews were conducted between August 2024 and November 2024. Subsequently, qualitative data analysis was performed according to Kuckartz and Rädiker using a deductive-inductive research approach. Results The results of this study showed that the methodological approach for selecting O&M in DTx studies was primarily based on research, as well as on personal prior experience and individual ideas. Interview participants indicated that when selecting O&M, they particularly focused on aspects such as scientific quality criteria or practical implementation and feasibility. A suggestion for achieving better comparability of DTx studies in the future was to use standardized O&M per therapeutic indication area. Almost all interviewees considered COS to be a suitable approach for improving the comparability of DTx and associated studies. However, we also identified critical perspectives that questioned their application. Conclusions Across professional groups, both commonalities and differences were observed in methodological approaches as well as in the selection of O&M in DTx studies. To improve the comparability of DTx interventions and trials, several approaches have been developed, for example, through the use of guidance frameworks, artificial intelligence programs, or the establishment of COS. However, further research is warranted to advance this field.

items.title: Self-Supervised One-Class Tabular Deep Learning for Intrusion Detection in Artificial Intelligence of Things Systems
items.abstract: The emergence of the artificial intelligence of things (AIoT) has led to increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks. For many of these threats, labeled training data are scarce or unavailable, which increases the need for label-free intrusion detection systems. To address this issue, this study proposes a self-supervised one-class TabNet framework, termed SS-OC-TabNet, for intrusion detection in tabular network traffic. The framework combines self-supervised representation learning and one-class compactness learning within a two-stage training process. In the first stage, masked-feature reconstruction is used to learn the feature structure of normal traffic from unlabeled data. In the second stage, a hypersphere compactness objective is applied to make the latent representations of normal traffic more compact for anomaly detection. TabNet is used as the backbone to support sequential feature selection, which also improves interpretability. The proposed model was evaluated on the NSL-KDD dataset and further validated through comparison with related works on the ToN-IoT dataset, achieving an accuracy of 93.20% with a false alarm rate of 2.13%. Further, the interpretability results show which traffic features influence the model's decisions. The compact design and low computational complexity of the proposed framework also support energy-efficient deployment in resource-constrained AIoT environments. These results indicate that SS-OC-TabNet is a viable tool for label-free intrusion detection in AIoT environments. items.title: Sex-specific electromyographic, performance, and symptomatic differences between sitting and cycling computer workstations
items.abstract: Studies suggest that computer workers may benefit from cycling workstations; however, little is known about the sex-specific mechanistic impacts of cycling on computer work-related risk factors. Twenty-six computer users (14 females) underwent two 60-min sessions of typing: one sitting, and one lightly cycling, while performance, symptoms and electromyography were recorded. Results show that males' typing speed was lower during cycling than sitting, while females' performance remained similar between conditions (Sex × Condition, p = 0.029). Neck/shoulder and visual discomfort were lower during cycling for both sexes, with females experiencing less neck/shoulder discomfort than males (Sex × Condition × Time, p = 0.006). Neck/shoulder muscle activation increased with time during sitting but decreased during cycling, especially in females. Low back muscle activity was higher during cycling, particularly in females (Sex × Condition × Time interaction, p = 0.046). Findings suggest sex-specific responses to cycling during computer work.

items.title: Shifting cognitive structures in human-AI collaborative learning design
items.abstract: This study examines collaborative learning design with a generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) co-pilot among in-service university English teachers in China. In a between-subjects experiment ( N = 60), epistemic network analysis (ENA) was used to model the situated discourse structures of team dialogues, complemented by thematic analysis of interviews. AI-supported teams achieved higher overall scores on a rubric covering constructive alignment, Universal Design for Learning principles, and other aspects of learning design. ENA identified task-specific differences in collaborative discourse, with AI-supported teams displaying a more interconnected and learner-centered network. Participants described the AI as a pedagogical conscience and an intellectual sparring partner whose prompts kept professional judgment visible during the design process. The findings suggest that, in complex professional tasks, GenAI may support reflection and pedagogical reasoning alongside design work.

items.title: Shipping in 76 Locales: A Multi-Case Study of LLM-Agent Localization Pipelines for Production Mobile Apps
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents translate software interfaces at scale, yet production evidence on what breaks—and which safeguards catch it—is nearly absent: a 2026 mapping study of localization testing retained 24 primary studies, though none on LLM-driven localization. We report a multi-case study of fourteen shipped mobile apps by one developer (ten iOS, four Android; 40–76 locales; roughly 347,000 units) at five maturity levels. Mining the repositories (catalogs, 4473 commits, process documents, tooling), we code defects into thirteen classes in two waves, the second under a frozen codebook, and map each to its detecting layer. Translation quality is not independently measured; the defect record is a lower bound. Of 468 commit-anchored defects, process and coverage gaps—strings escaping the pipeline—are modal in each wave (26.7% and 27.5%); placeholder errors are near-absent (9 in 347,000 units). LLM judges are the largest operational detector (26.7%), ahead of humans (16.0%) and validators (13.7%), yet 127 defects (27.1%) escaped every layer until our audit. What escapes tracks validator scope, not maturity alone. Layered validation, not prompt-level care, determines what reaches users. Translation takes minutes; the validation stack is the lasting cost. We derive six testable propositions and ten guidelines, and release the codebook, dataset, and scripts.

items.title: Shortcut Sensitivity in Agent-Safety Evaluations
items.abstract: AI agents take actions through tools. Some actions are sensitive, so guards that supervise them must themselves be evaluated reliably. Yet the data used to evaluate a guard can include cues that make labels predictable without measuring the intended safety construct, and those cues can also influence guard decisions. We introduce a three-level shortcut-auditing framework and audit completed LinuxArena trajectories and two TS-Bench-derived step datasets. We distinguish label predictability, observational guard association, and paired decision sensitivity. In LinuxArena, shorter average shell commands strongly predict trajectory labels. In AgentDojo-Traj, exact-tool lookup falls from F_1=.901 with mixed-domain folds to .495 under domain holdout. In AgentHarm-Traj, released TS-Guard F_1 falls from .902 under row weighting to .719 with equal interaction weighting, while balanced accuracy rises. We then test the strongest safe-row marker association in a seven-configuration screen on a frozen 64-step AgentDojo-Traj cohort using repeated, interleaved Haiku calls. Rewriting the marker lowers blocking by 8.33 percentage points, while opaque tool aliases raise it by 11.46 points. All unsafe calls remain blocked; the changes concern false positives against inherited labels. Both effects remain nonzero after subtracting the formatting-placebo effect, with exploratory 95% ranges excluding zero. The same edits also change measured accuracy against inherited labels. This provides direct evidence that benchmark representation can materially change a guard's decisions and measured evaluation performance. The Haiku-sized effects do not reproduce in Luna or deterministic Q8 TS-Guard. We recommend domain group holdouts, evaluation-unit metrics, and placebo-controlled paired interventions.

items.abstract: RSUP dr. Sitanala is committed to strengthening patient safety culture toward a smart hospital paradigm through an artificial intelligence (AI)-driven innovation named Si Aman EduBot. This interactive chatbot, integrated via WhatsApp and the hospital's proprietary application, was developed to provide real-time education on safety standards, emergency procedures, and digital incident reporting systems for both staff and patients. This study aims to evaluate the impact of Si Aman EduBot implementation on enhancing safety culture within the hospital environment. The evaluation results over a three-month period demonstrated significant achievements, including over 5,000 user interactions, a 35% increase in incident reporting volume, and a 20% improvement in patient safety culture scores from the baseline. The rapid and responsive nature of the chatbot proved effective in increasing staff awareness and fostering an open, blame-free reporting culture. Through its interactive educational features and digital system integration, Si Aman EduBot holds the potential to serve as a national model for building a sustainable patient safety culture. Future developments will focus on integrating voice assistant capabilities and electronic medical records. items.title: Smart Ads-Smart Ads for Smart City
items.abstract: Traditional advertising methods, such as paper posters, banners, and hoardings, require manual design, printing, installation, and maintenance. These activities increase operational effort, material consumption, and the difficulty of updating advertisements. This paper presents SmartAds, a web-based artificial intelligence-powered digital advertisement management platform developed to simplify advertisement creation, pricing, payment-record management, approval, scheduling, and display. The system enables users to generate promotional descriptions and slogans from product details using large language model services. A fallback mechanism involving Groq, an optional local Ollama model, and rule-based generation supports content creation when an AI service is unavailable. Users can select poster or video formats, choose display slots, calculate advertisement costs, and track their submissions. Administrators can approve or reject advertisements before they are scheduled for display. The platform also includes payment-record management, receipt generation, notifications, optional AI avatar-video generation through D-ID, and a browser-based virtual LED display. SmartAds was implemented using Python, Flask, SQLAlchemy, HTML, Bootstrap, and JavaScript. Functional testing documented in the project report covered 45 test cases, all reported as passing. The system demonstrates the feasibility of integrating AI-assisted content generation with digital advertisement workflow management in a controlled proof-of-concept environment.

items.title: Social and Structural Determinants of Chronic Pain Among Migrant Workers: A Scoping Review Using an Intersectionality Framework
items.abstract: Background: Due to structural inequities, many migrant workers face adverse health outcomes potentially exposing them to long-term pain issues. However, the extent of current knowledge on chronic pain (>3 months) in this population is unclear. As labor migration policies evolve toward less protective measures, it is essential to gain insights into the experiences and drivers of chronic pain among migrant workers. Aims: Drawing on the theoretical framework of intersectionality, this scoping review aimed to synthesize existing knowledge on chronic pain among migrant workers in Canada and the United States. More precisely, we examined evidence related to epidemiology, treatments, lived experiences, and the role of social and structural determinants. Methods: This review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology for scoping reviews. A search of four databases was followed by a screening and extraction procedure involving four researchers. Relevant findings were reported through quantified and narrative syntheses. Results: This scoping review highlights a major gap in understanding pain chronicity among migrant workers. Nine studies met the eligibility criteria. Most studies have focused on occupational health outcomes. Definitions of chronic pain are inconsistent. Only one qualitative study examined migrant workers' pain trajectories beyond workplace settings. Social and structural determinants were underscored in all studies, including poor working conditions, socioeconomic precarity, unfavorable labor market structure, restrictive immigration policies, racism and discrimination, and gendered inequities. Conclusions: This review invites researchers and policymakers to move beyond occupational health approaches to fully appraise and tackle the intersecting structural and political drivers exposing migrant workers to lifelong experiences of chronic pain.

items.title: Social Networking Usage, Informal Workplace Learning and Personal Professional Development: A Structural Equation Model on the Teachers’ Attitudes and Beliefs towards ICT Adoption in Public Schools
items.abstract: The objective of this study was to determine the influence of social networking use, informal workplace learning, and personal professional development on teachers' attitudes and beliefs towards ICT adoption among public secondary school teachers in Region XI, Philippines. Standardized survey questionnaires were adopted and contextualized to suit the regional educational setting. The instruments were administered to 417 randomly selected teachers using stratified random sampling. This study employed a quantitative, non-experimental research design, using means, Pearson's r, and Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) for data analysis. The results revealed generally low to very low levels of social networking usage, informal workplace learning, personal professional development, and attitudes and beliefs toward ICT adoption. Despite these modest levels, significant positive relationships were found between social networking use and teachers' attitudes toward ICT adoption, as well as between personal professional development and these attitudes. Furthermore, the structural equation modeling results indicated that the three independent variables significantly influenced teachers' attitudes and beliefs toward ICT adoption, with social networking usage emerging as the strongest predictor among the constructs. The findings underscore the importance of enhancing digital engagement, strengthening informal learning cultures, and providing sustained professional development initiatives to foster more positive attitudes and stronger readiness for ICT integration in schools.

items.title: Socioeconomic determinants of academic motivation in higher education: A systematic review and critical synthesis of international evidence
items.abstract: Academic motivation in higher education constitutes a multidimensional construct shaped by structural conditions that influence students’ academic performance, persistence, and educational trajectories. In contexts characterized by persistent social inequalities, understanding how socioeconomic status (SES) configures motivational processes is essential for the development of university policies aimed at equity and educational sustainability. The purpose of this study was to conduct a critical synthesis of international evidence on the mechanisms through which socioeconomic factors influences academic motivation in higher education during the period period 2017–2020 and 2022–2025. A systematic review was carried out in accordance with PRISMA guidelines to ensure methodological rigor, transparency, and replicability. The literature search was conducted in the Scopus database using structured Boolean search equations. After applying predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, 33 empirical studies were selected for the final analysis. The results of the systematic synthesis reveal sustained growth in scientific output and progressive geographic diversification of the field. Cross-sectional quantitative studies predominate, employing regression models and structural analyses to examine the relationship between parental educational level, financial support, and intrinsic motivation or academic engagement. In addition, several studies incorporate mediating variables such as self-efficacy, institutional integration, and sense of belonging, revealing non-linear explanatory configurations. Overall, the evidence indicates that the influence of socioeconomic status operates through both direct and indirect mechanisms linked to cultural capital and institutional resources. This review identifies key theoretical convergences as well as recurrent methodological limitations within the field. Finally, the findings underscore the need for longitudinal studies and multilevel approaches to deepen the understanding of motivational inequalities in higher education.

items.title: Solid Lipid Nanoparticles and Nanostructured Lipid Carriers in Drug Delivery: A Review
items.abstract: Many pharmacological compounds suffer from poor aqueous solubility, variable bioavailability, fast degradation, unfavorable biodistribution and dose-related side effects, which restrict their therapeutic efficacy. Conventional dosage forms may not achieve the appropriate drug concentrations within the therapeutic window, necessitating the development of improved delivery platforms. Lipid-based nanocarriers, especially solid lipid nanoparticles (SLNs) and nanostructured lipid carriers (NLCs), provide intriguing methods owing to their biocompatibility, biodegradability and formulation diversity. SLNs are composed of a largely solid lipid matrix supported by surfactants, while NLCs are a mixture of solid and liquid lipids that form a less ordered matrix with more drug accommodation and less drug ejection during storage. This review critically discusses recent advances, with emphasis on literature published during 2021–2026, on the evolution, classification, structural characteristics, formulation components, preparation and characterization, drug-loading and release mechanisms, biological fate, surface engineering, administration routes, and therapeutic applications of SLNs and NLCs. Special attention is paid to safety, regulatory issues, scale-up, commercialization and emerging technologies including artificial intelligence-assisted optimization and microfluidic production. [There has been] considerable preclinical progress but little clinical translation. Long term stability, reproducible large scale manufacturing, regulatory uniformity, and rigorous clinical validation are significant difficulties that need to be systematically investigated.

items.title: SpaceMates: A Tabletop Robotic Tangible Programming System Designed to Cultivate Spatial Reasoning Skills in Middle Childhood
items.abstract: Spatial reasoning is a key cognitive foundation for children’s STEM learning, yet existing tools focus on 2D tasks or programming logic, with limited integration of multidimensional spatial reasoning, embodied interaction, and feedback. We developed SpaceMates, a tangible programming game combining tabletop robots with 3D-printed blocks for children aged 7–10. Children construct 3D structures, plan routes with height variations, and compare intended and executed paths through robot feedback. Based on developmental trajectories of spatial skills in middle childhood and the Spatial Reasoning Instrument (SRI), we designed tasks for ages 7–8 and 9–10. In study with 30 participants, we examined within- and between-condition changes. Unadjusted tests suggested MR and SV gains for ages 7–8 and SO gains for ages 9–10 in SpaceMates, with greater SO gains than Baseline. In Holm-adjusted analyses, only the pre–post SO change among participants aged 9–10 remained statistically significant; after adjustment, no between-condition gain comparison remained statistically significant. Behavioral analyses characterized interaction patterns.

items.title: Strategic AI Integration in Higher Education
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence in higher education is occurring at a rapid pace and institutions are still playing catch-up with piecemeal strategies. This chapter presents a governance model that integrates artificial intelligence into curricula, teaching practices, ethical considerations and student learning outcomes. The work is informed by recent research on adaptive learning systems, algorithmic accountability, and outcome-based education (OBE). The model places emphasis on four key elements: curriculum design, faculty training, student data management and institutional governance, outlining roles and decision-making processes. The argument is clear. The incorporation of AI is not a technical issue The framework presented here is grounded in current literature from 2020 to 2024 and incorporates evidence from global pilot programmes in the US, United Kingdom, Australia and India. The chapter concludes that sustainable AI integration depends not on the sophistication of the tools deployed but on the quality of the human decisions made around them.

items.title: Stress and self-efficacy under artificial intelligence disruption: A mixed-methods study on the usage of artificial intelligence among Finnish workers
items.abstract: Rapid workplace integration of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping work practices and challenging employees’ self-efficacy and well-being. This mixed-methods study examines these experiences using national survey data ( N = 2109) and qualitative interviews ( N = 54) with Finnish workers. Frequent AI use, AI-induced identity threat, and organizational AI deployment are associated with higher AI strain, whereas AI self-efficacy relates to frequent use, positive AI attitudes, and subjective well-being. Identity threat moderated several of these associations, highlighting the role of professional identity in AI-related experiences. Analysis drawing on Greimas’ semiotic modalities (must, can, know, and want) explains how these patterns are interpreted and negotiated in practice, revealing tensions between perceived self-efficacy and pressures to integrate AI. AI use was often described as voluntary. However, participants anticipated increasing competence demands and responsibility. The findings emphasize the need for organizational strategies that address identity-related challenges and support employee well-being in AI-driven work transformations.

items.title: Surgeon-Derived Design Insights Regarding Real-Time Artificial Intelligence Decision Support for Endoscopic Cancer Surgery
items.abstract: Introduction Real-time artificial intelligence (AI) decision-support systems are increasingly proposed for use in endoscopic and minimally invasive surgery although how best to present such information intraoperatively is unclear. This study explored surgeon perspectives regarding the user-interface, interpretation and workflow integration of a prototype AI system (CLASSICA-OR) for real-time endoscopic cancer characterization during surgery. Methods Surgeons specialising in minimally invasive gastrointestinal surgery were asked for their first impressions in their evaluation of the CLASSICA-OR system within a high-fidelity surgical simulation environment. For this, participants viewed prerecorded colonoscopic imagery of significant rectal neoplasia while the AI analysis was applied in real-time to the video. Commentary and responses to semi-structured interview were recorded audiovisually for transcription and analysis using qualitative thematic analysis supported by NVivo (Lumivero). Results Eighteen surgeons participated, generating rich qualitative data. Four major themes emerged: (1) AI was viewed as a valuable but evolving decision-support tool; (2) institutional culture, governance and commercial realities were recognised as important determinants of adoption; (3) real-time perfusion-based lesion characterisation (foundational to CLASSICA-OR) was considered promising but with specific challenges; and (4) clarity, usability, transparency and workflow compatibility are surgeon priorities in decision-support displays. Participants emphasised minimised cognitive load, preserved surgeon autonomy, clear communication of uncertainty and seamless workflow integration. Preferences differed between simplified binary outputs and more detailed numerical displays supporting the need for adaptable interfaces. Conclusions Surgeons perceive real-time intraoperative AI decision support as promising but requiring thoughtful user-centred design. They articulate practical development and implementation insights for intraoperative AI systems.

items.title: Sustainability and Women's Empowerment Through Technology
items.abstract: Technological change is a major development agent across all the layers of contemporary societies, from how economies work to how people access information, how social life is conducted, and even how political institutions work and how decisions are made. In the twenty-first century, digital technologies, ranging from artificial intelligence to mobile connectivity to financial technology and blockchain applications, have revolutionized markets, knowledge, social life, and even the nature of political participation. Sustainability and gender equality, meanwhile, have become twin planks of development frameworks worldwide. The agency of women and girls has been recognized as a transformative force in the development process, and empowerment is understood as central to progress. In turn, gender equality is linked to enhanced economic productivity, poverty reduction, and sustainability. Digital technologies have opened up new paths for women in education, entrepreneurship, employment, and participation. They have helped to reduce some of the traditional structural constraints by expanding women’s access to credit, networks, and information, thereby unleashing the power of women’s agency. But this is far from being the whole story. Women’s access to, skills in using, and power to drive innovation through technology are unequal worldwide. Women’s talent is acutely under-represented in tech-powered jobs, and the digital gender gap constrains women’s empowerment in the digital economy. This chapter explores how sustainability and women’s empowerment through technology relate to each other, with a focus on the Brazilian case, and brings to light some of the key opportunities and challenges.

items.title: Sustainability of complex interventions in long-term care homes: a scoping review
items.abstract: This is a scoping review protocol that aims to map and characterize the available evidence on the sustainability of complex interventions implemented in long-term care homes. This study adheres to the PRISMA-ScR guidelines and the JBI recommendations for scoping reviews. Searches will be conducted across five electronic databases (MEDLINE, CINAHL, Web of Science, Embase, and LILACS) from inception onward, covering six languages (English, Portuguese, Spanish, French, Italian, and German). Primary research studies (quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods) describing sustainable complex interventions in long-term care homes will be eligible. Two reviewers will independently perform study selection and data extraction, utilizing human-supervised artificial intelligence (AI) tools within Covidence to support screening and data audit workflows. Extracted data will be synthesized using descriptive statistics, narrative synthesis, and qualitative content analysis. Identified barriers and facilitators will be inductively extracted and deductively coded into domains of the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research. Depending on the volume of data retrieved, findings may be published across multiple papers.

items.title: Sustainable Development and Environmental Impact: The Role of AI in Circular Economy in the Construction Industry Era 6.0
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly studied in construction, but its integration with the Circular Economy (CE) remains insufficiently explored. This study maps AI-related construction research and examines its implications for CE within the context of Industry 6.0. A bibliometric analysis of Scopus publications from 2014 to 2024 was conducted using Microsoft Excel and VOSviewer to analyze publication trends, keyword co-occurrence, country contributions, and author productivity. Artificial Intelligence was the dominant keyword, with 291 occurrences, followed by Construction Industry (129), Machine Learning (68), and Sustainable Development (52). China contributed the most publications, while research activity increased substantially after 2020. The findings highlight AI’s potential to support material prediction, waste reduction, material tracking, reuse, and recycling. However, stronger integration of AI research with measurable CE outcomes remains necessary. Future studies should evaluate AI-enabled circular construction using indicators of material efficiency, waste prevention, and resource recovery.

items.title: Synergizing physical and cognitive training toward active aging with mixed reality
items.abstract: The aging of the global population poses a growing challenge to healthcare systems, as increased longevity is often accompanied by progressive physical and cognitive decline. In the absence of disease-modifying treatments, Active Aging (AA) is promoted as a strategy to preserve autonomy and quality of life through sustained physical, cognitive, and social engagement. While technologies such as extended reality and social robots have already been adopted to support physical training, delivering scalable and engaging cognitive interventions in everyday environments remains an open problem. This paper is grounded in the vision of a holistic Dual-Layer Intervention Framework, in which physical and cognitive training are tightly integrated through embodied interactive systems. Within this broader vision, we present the design and implementation of a Cognitive Intervention Layer based on a large language model–driven conversational agent, deployed on a mixed reality (MR) platform. The proposed solution delivers reminiscence therapy through natural verbal interaction, grounded in the user's physical environment and personal belongings, and is designed to seamlessly interoperate with an existing MR-based Physical Intervention Layer. Preliminary validation through pilot user studies demonstrates the feasibility and usability of the proposed approach, indicating that visually grounded, technology-mediated reminiscence can be effectively integrated into home-based AA routines.

items.title: System1-Arena: Which Decisions Can Be Left to System 1?
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often make discrete decisions, such as flagging phishing or escalating to a human. System-1 models, such as Jev and the OpenAI Decisions API, return probabilities over options in a single forward pass, while System-2 approaches generate reasoning steps. Which decisions can System-1 models handle, and which require generative reasoning? We introduce System1-Arena, a benchmark that gives all models the same decision requests and scores their probabilities. It contains 92k questions across 105 tasks from 268 public sources, in four groups: text classification and knowledge, applied decisions, evaluation and control, and agent and action. It also includes 138 closed-loop environments, from web shopping and SWE-bench coding control to robotics, games, and driving; in real-time mode, the world evolves while a model decides. We evaluate 30 models: 7 closed LLMs, 13 open LLMs read at the answer token, and 10 System-1 models. The largest System-1 models match or exceed fast closed LLMs in non-agentic accuracy, with better-calibrated probabilities at one-quarter of the latency. A reasoning LLM is the most accurate, at about 70x the cost of a fast LLM. In closed loops, large open LLMs succeed most often (up to 32.9%); small System-1 models rarely succeed.

items.title: Systematic Review Using Artificial Intelligence: From Planning to Evidence Synthesis
items.abstract: Systematic reviews are widely regarded as the cornerstone of evidence-based medicine and decision-making, providing structured, transparent, and reproducible syntheses of the available research evidence on a given question. However, traditional systematic review methodologies were developed in an era of comparatively modest scholarly output and now face an evidence base that doubles in size at intervals of less than a decade. The average review requires well over a year of collaborative work, involves screening thousands of records, and relies on manual, cognitively demanding procedures that scale poorly with the volume, velocity, and heterogeneity of contemporary scientific literature. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning, natural language processing, and, more recently, large language models (LLMs), has emerged as a promising response to this challenge of scale. This thesis presents a comprehensive, end-to-end examination of the application of AI throughout the systematic review lifecycle, structured around the four canonical phases of the review workflow: planning; search and study selection; data extraction and critical appraisal; and evidence synthesis and reporting. Drawing on more than two hundred primary sources, including methodological standards established by Cochrane, the PRISMA 2020 statement, five decades of AI research, and empirical studies on the automation of evidence synthesis published between 2006 and 2025, this thesis examines the capabilities and limitations of different classes of AI methods at each stage of the review process. Classical machine learning approaches to relevance screening, supported by two decades of evaluation evidence and shown to reduce screening workload while maintaining high recall, are distinguished from prompt-based LLM approaches. The latter offer broader capabilities, including search query formulation, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment, but their reliability remains insufficient to support unsupervised deployment in rigorous evidence synthesis. The thesis develops a unified analytical framework that maps AI capabilities onto the different phases of systematic reviews; consolidates empirical evidence concerning performance, workload reduction, and failure modes; situates these technologies within Cochrane's methodological standards, the PRISMA 2020 reporting framework, and emerging guidance on the responsible use of generative AI in research; and examines the ethical, epistemological, and organisational implications of delegating knowledge-related tasks to machines. The findings indicate that AI is neither a substitute for the methodological rigour required by systematic reviews nor merely a peripheral convenience. Rather, it constitutes a potentially transformative assistive infrastructure whose safe and effective implementation depends on human-in-the-loop architectures, phase-specific validation, transparent reporting of automation procedures, and the preservation of human judgement as the ultimate authority in evaluating and substantiating knowledge claims. The thesis concludes by presenting structured recommendations for systematic review teams, technology developers, academic journals, and policymakers. It also proposes a research agenda for the emerging field of AI-native evidence synthesis, emphasising the need for rigorous evaluation, methodological transparency, responsible governance, and the continued integration of human expertise into increasingly automated research workflows.

items.title: Systems Learning
items.abstract: This chapter introduces Systems Learning as a practical management discipline for continuously understanding and refining organizational performance in complex adaptive systems. Rather than treating learning as an activity reserved for failures or formal investigations, the chapter presents Systems Learning as an ongoing management mindset focused on discovering gaps between work-as-done and work-as-imagined/planned, understanding the organizational structures producing those gaps, and realigning the system to better achieve its intended purposes. Drawing from systems thinking, resilience engineering, and operational experience, the chapter introduces the Systems Learning Framework consisting of Discovery, Understanding, and Realignment. Together, these iterative processes help managers remain connected to operational reality, recognize meaningful patterns, interpret weak signals, infer operating point movement, and identify structural conditions shaping human performance. Discovery emphasizes learning from normal work as well as failure. The chapter explores organizational intelligence as an emergent capability arising through interaction, feedback, communication, interpretation, and shared understanding distributed throughout the system. It also emphasizes continual system tune-ups that realign organizational structure to strengthen adaptive capacity, resilience, and the organization’s ability to respond effectively as conditions evolve.

items.title: Systems Thinking
items.abstract: This chapter introduces systems thinking as a practical management discipline for understanding how organizational systems shape human performance, operational outcomes, and risk. The chapter explains that workplace behavior cannot be understood through isolated events or individual actions alone. Managers must instead examine the interactions, feedback loops, constraints, assumptions, and organizational influences that continuously shape work-as-done under changing operational conditions. Using the Iceberg Model as a guiding framework, the chapter demonstrates how visible events emerge from deeper patterns, structures, assumptions, and mental models distributed throughout the organization. The chapter emphasizes that pattern recognition often precedes understanding and that systems thinking helps managers develop organizational intelligence through operational feedback, shared experience, communication, observation, interpretation, and continual interaction across organizational functions. Practical Systems Thinking Tools – second stories, mindmapping, behavior-over-time charts, causal loop diagrams, stock-and-flow diagrams, AcciMaps, FRAM, STAMP, and Stream Analysis – are described to help managers visualize interactions, identify leverage points, recognize weak signals, and better understand operating point movement. Throughout the chapter, emphasis is placed on adaptation, drift, local rationality, and understanding how interactions within organizational systems influence resilience, learning, safety, reliability, and operational effectiveness.

items.title: Talent Management and Work Design in an Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Future
items.abstract: The advancement of 4IR technologies, notably artificial Intelligence (AI), has contributed to shaping the new world of work. The contemporary workplace is characterised by various forms of digital technology that enable employees to work from anywhere and at any time. The convergence of talent management, work design, and AI signifies a vital change in how organisations approach their operational frameworks and workforce strategies. Talent management refers to the systematic process of attracting, developing, and retaining skilled and high-potential employees within an organisation. Work design is the process of organising and structuring tasks, activities, and responsibilities within a job or a workplace. This chapter examines how AI, talent management, and work design may work together to alter the workplace, improve employee well-being, and help organisations to remain competitive in an increasingly complex and fast-paced world of work.

items.title: Task Motivation, Task Emotions, and Cognitive Engagement in L2 Oral Tasks: The Case of Chinese Post-Secondary L2 Learners of English
items.abstract: Drawing on control-value theory and situated expectancy-value theory, this study investigated the relationships between task motivation (i.e., expectancy for success, task values, and task cost), task emotions (i.e., task enjoyment and task anxiety), and cognitive engagement in L2 oral tasks among Chinese post-secondary English learners. A total of 308 Chinese post-secondary students participated in the L2 oral task and completed the task motivation and task emotions questionnaires. Path analysis showed that task value positively predicted learners’ cognitive engagement, and task cost negatively predicted it. While expectancy for success did not predict cognitive engagement directly, its effect was fully mediated by task enjoyment and anxiety. The results also revealed that task anxiety partially mediated the relationships between the other two dimensions of task motivation (task value and task cost) and cognitive engagement. These findings highlight the intricate relationships between motivation, emotions, and cognitive engagement in task-based language teaching, offering both valuable theoretical insights and practical implications for L2 education.

items.title: Taylorism reloaded?
items.abstract: The diffusion of artificial intelligence, data analytics and digital technologies in manufacturing has revived debates about the impact of technological change on work and employment relations. This article examines the implementation of Industry 4.0 technologies in a Spanish train manufacturing company and analyses their implications for workers and their representatives. Drawing on Labour Process Theory and industrial relations literature, the study is based on a qualitative case study including interviews with workers, works council members and technical staff. The findings show that the transition to Industry 4.0 primarily involved the implementation of a Manufacturing Execution System (MES), which digitalised production processes and data collection. Rather than increasing worker autonomy, the system reinforced Taylorist principles through greater standardisation, monitoring and performance measurement. The study also finds that worker representatives played a limited role in regulating technological change despite the existence of formal information and consultation rights. The article argues that technological opacity, institutional constraints and the prioritisation of traditional bargaining issues limit the capacity of worker representatives to influence the governance of workplace technologies.

items.title: Teacher Readiness for Human-Centred AI Integration in Higher Education: Evidence from Assam, India
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming higher education, making teacher readiness essential for responsible integration. This paper proposes an empirical framework to examine higher education teachers’ readiness for human-centred AI integration in Assam. Based on UNESCO’s AI Competency Framework for Teachers, the study focuses on five dimensions: human-centred mindset, AI ethics, AI foundations and applications, AI pedagogy, and AI-supported professional learning, alongside institutional support. A quantitative, cross-sectional survey design is proposed, employing a structured questionnaire and statistical analyses to assess readiness and its influencing factors. Addressing a regional research gap, the study emphasises ethical judgment, pedagogical competence, and human accountability rather than technological adoption alone. As primary data collection is pending, the framework provides a basis for future empirical investigation. The anticipated findings may inform faculty development, institutional AI policies, and responsible AI integration in higher education.

items.title: Technology Is Not the Treatment: An Integrative Clinical Reasoning Framework for Technology-Enhanced Rehabilitation
items.abstract: Digital technology has been used in rehabilitation for decades, from early electronic games and computer-based cognitive training to contemporary virtual and augmented reality, exergaming, robotics, wearables, telerehabilitation, and artificial-intelligence-enabled systems. The field has therefore moved well beyond the question of whether technology can be used in rehabilitation. Existing frameworks address important parts of the problem, including treatment specification, technology classification and selection, therapeutic gaming and virtual-reality decision making, technology-specific clinical utilization, design, adoption, implementation, and co-development. Rather than claiming that these elements are new, this paper asks whether they can be integrated into a technology-agnostic point-of-care reasoning architecture. The Technology-Enhanced Rehabilitation (TER) Framework begins with therapeutic intent: a meaningful goal, an explicit therapeutic target, and a plausible therapeutic strategy. Technology then passes through a therapeutic value checkpoint and may be rejected when a reasonable non-technological alternative is preferable. When technology is justified, clinicians identify the required technological capability, assess fit across person, clinician, technology, and context, and deliberately configure a patient-specific therapeutic experience. TER distinguishes external/technology load, internal response, and a provisional concept of target-relevant therapeutic exposure within an iterative dose-response-adjustment loop. Realized therapeutic value is ultimately judged by meaningful transfer, not technology-native performance. TER is proposed to complement and connect, rather than replace, existing rehabilitation, technology-specific, design, and implementation frameworks.

items.title: Technology-Enhanced Language Instruction for Economics Students
items.abstract: For economics students today who want to pursue careers in international business, finance, entrepreneurship, and economic policy in the globalized economy, efficient communication in English is a vital skill. Many students grasp English grammar and vocabular y, but they struggle to acquire the speaking abilities required for professional communication. Speaking anxiety, lack of genuine engagement, lack of business-related terminology, and weak confidence still impair learners’ speaking performance. At the same time, however, technological advancement has transformed language education by creating new options for communication, cooperation, and customized learning. The work under review is devoted to innovative methods of developing the professional speaking skills of economics students through the use of Communicative Language Teaching (CLT) and educational technology. The review of studies on speaking training, communicative competence, technology-enhanced language learning, gamification, artificial intelligence, and professional communication in higher education is included in the study. Special focus is paid to the utilization of digital platforms, online collaboration tools, gamified learning settings (e.g., Kahoot), and AI-assisted language learning tools that enhance speaking development. The study shows a favorable influence of communicative and technology-based strategies on speaking fluency, student engagement, communicative confidence, and the capacity to communicate in a professional manner. Results also show that the use of CLT principles and digital learning tools can provide tremendous opportunities for economics students to practice business communication in real and interactive scenarios. The paper ends with a discussion of the pedagogical implications for higher education institutions and suggestions for the future of technology-enhanced speaking training in economics education.

items.title: Tennis Participation Across the Lifespan: Functional and Biological Adaptations Relevant to Healthy Aging
items.abstract: Maintaining physiological function, mobility, and independence throughout aging remains a major challenge in exercise and health sciences. Physical activity is widely recognized as a key determinant of healthy aging, yet different sports may confer distinct biological benefits. Tennis is unique in that it combines aerobic and anaerobic exercise, neuromuscular coordination, cognitive engagement, perceptual demands, and functional movement demands (balance, agility, change-of-direction performance, motor coordination) within a single activity. This comprehensive review synthesizes current evidence regarding the biological adaptations associated with tennis participation across the lifespan and evaluates its potential contribution to healthy aging and longevity. Available evidence indicates that regular tennis participation is associated with improved cardiovascular and cardiometabolic health, enhanced musculoskeletal function, greater bone mineral density, maintenance of cognitive and perceptual abilities, and improved psychological well-being. Studies involving veteran and masters tennis players further suggest that long-term participation may attenuate age-related declines in physical and cognitive function while supporting successful aging and quality of life. Emerging research also highlights potential benefits related to neuromuscular function, sensorimotor performance, perceptual-cognitive abilities and functional independence. Collectively, the literature supports tennis as a multidimensional lifelong physical activity capable of promoting health across biological, psychological, and social domains. While much of the current evidence remains observational, the available literature consistently suggests that tennis participation is associated with adaptations relevant to healthy aging and functional health. Further longitudinal studies are needed to clarify the underlying mechanisms and strengthen evidence-based recommendations for healthy aging, maintenance of physical function, and preservation of mobility across the lifespan.

items.title: The AI Mirror: A Qualitative Study of Student Autonomy and Dependence in ESL Writing
items.abstract: This article explores the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in English as a Second Language (ESL) writing, examining whether it fosters autonomy or promotes dependency. Utilizing a qualitative methodology, semi-structured interviews were conducted following a timed writing task with 40 intermediate-level ESL students across three higher education institutions in Oman. Thematic analysis reveals that AI's impact on student autonomy is highly contingent upon its pedagogical application. When utilized strategically for brainstorming and personalized feedback, AI acts as a scaffolding tool that fosters self-directed learning. Conversely, when students rely on AI to generate complete texts or passively correct errors, they experience cognitive offloading, leading to decreased independence. The study emphasizes the need for educators to cultivate digital literacy, promoting an approach that empowers students to use AI as an intellectual partner rather than a cognitive replacement.

items.title: THE ANCHORING EFFECT IN AI-ASSISTED DECISION-MAKING: HOW INITIAL RECOMMENDATIONS SHAPE HUMAN JUDGMENT
items.abstract: Abstract Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is intended to make algorithmic outputs more understandable, auditable, and contestable. Yet an explanation does not reach a neutral observer: people interpret it through prior beliefs, cognitive shortcuts, professional experience, and assumptions about machine competence. This conceptual paper examines how cognitive biases shape the interpretation of XAI and why greater transparency does not necessarily produce better decisions. Drawing on research on automation bias, judgment and decision-making, explainability, and human–AI collaboration, the paper develops an integrative framework linking explanation characteristics, user cognition, task context, and reliance behavior. It argues that anchoring, confirmation bias, availability, authority effects, and cognitive miserliness can transform explanations into persuasive cues rather than evidence for independent evaluation. Explanations may improve mental models and error detection when they are faithful, appropriately scoped, and matched to users’ needs; however, they may also legitimize an incorrect prediction, increase cognitive load, or create an illusion of understanding. The paper proposes design principles centered on calibrated trust, contrastive and uncertainty-aware explanations, independent judgment, verification prompts, and evaluation of decision quality rather than satisfaction alone. Because this is a conceptual synthesis rather than an empirical study, its propositions require experimental testing across domains and user groups. The central conclusion is that responsible XAI must design not only for model transparency but also for the cognitive conditions under which people interpret explanations. Keywords: explainable artificial intelligence, cognitive bias, automation bias, human–AI interaction, trust calibration, decision-making, algorithmic transparency

items.title: The Application of Artificial Intelligence in Brucellosis: Diagnosis, Genomic Analysis, Epidemiological Prediction and Drug Discovery
items.abstract: Brucellosis, a globally significant zoonosis caused by Brucella, poses a substantial impediment to the sustainable development of the livestock industry and threatens public health security. Traditional control and prevention strategies for brucellosis suffer from fundamental limitations. These include the time-consuming, biosafety risks associated with bacterial culture and the difficulty in differentiating between natural infection and vaccine-induced immunity with serological tests. There remains a challenge in accurately distinguishing vaccine strains from wild-type strains via genotyping methods. Furthermore, current practice relies on manual reporting and empirical judgment without real-time data support. Consequently, these challenges could hinder early detection and reduce the efficiency of large-scale screening, which leads to imprecise outbreak tracing and fails to meet the practical demands of modern livestock production for rapid diagnosis, intelligent prevention and control. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) technologies have been widely applied in the field of veterinary microbiology, which could offer novel technical pathways for the prevention and control of brucellosis. This paper reviews the latest research progress in the application of AI for the rapid diagnosis of brucellosis, genomic analysis and antimicrobial resistance prediction of Brucella, epidemiological risk early warning and the development of drugs and vaccines. We further analyze the current limitations of AI in brucellosis research including the scarcity of high-quality, annotated datasets, insufficient model interpretability and low efficiency in on-site translation and implementation. The paper provides an outlook on the future development of AI-based intelligent prevention and control systems for brucellosis, which offer a theoretical reference and innovative perspectives for the fundamental research and clinical application of AI technologies. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first review to integrate AI applications across the entire chain of brucellosis prevention and control and to propose a conceptual framework for AI-driven intelligent brucellosis management.

items.title: The Association Between Screen Time and Text Neck Syndrome Among Adolescence: A Cross-Sectional Study
items.abstract: Introduction: Text Neck Syndrome, coined by Dr. Dean L. Fishman (2008), is a modern musculoskeletal disorder caused by prolonged forward neck flexion during smartphone and device use. This posture increases cervical strain, leading to pain, stiffness, and postural deformities. Preventive strategies include ergonomic awareness, posture correction, and strengthening of neck muscles. Objective: To investigate the correlation between daily screen time and the severity of Text Neck Syndrome among Indian adolescents and to investigate the correlation between daily screen time and the disability of the neck Method: A cross-sectional observational study was conducted among 123 adolescents (aged 16–18 years) from selected schools and colleges in Bengaluru, India, using stratified random sampling. Ethical approval and informed consent were obtained. Data included demographic details, screen time screenshots, and responses to two validated tools: the Neck Disability Index (NDI) and Smartphone Addiction Scale–Short Version (SAS-SV). NDI assessed neck-related functional disability, while SAS-SV measured smartphone addiction levels. Participants were categorized into three screen time groups: 0–5, 5.1–10, and >10 hours per day. Data were analyzed using SPSS version 23.0 to examine associations between screen time, text neck symptoms, and neck disability. Results: Means and standard deviations summarized continuous variables; frequencies and percentages described categorical data. Independent t-tests and ANOVA assessed relationships between screen time, smartphone addiction (SAS), and neck disability (NDI). Results showed no statistically significant association (p > 0.05) between screen time, addiction, and neck disability. Discussion: This study investigated the association between screen time, smartphone addiction (SAS), and neck disability (NDI) in adolescents. Although prior research demonstrates that prolonged smartphone use increases neck pain and musculoskeletal risk, our findings showed no significant relationship between total screen time and neck disability. However, longer screen exposure was associated with higher smartphone addiction scores, indicating behavioral dependency. Biomechanical strain from sustained forward head posture and poor ergonomics may contribute to musculoskeletal issues over time. These results highlight the importance of combining ergonomic education, postural awareness, and behavioral interventions to reduce smartphone addiction and mitigate potential long-term physical and psychosocial health risks.

items.title: The Benefit–Sacrifice Trade-Off of AI-Powered Fashion Services: Effects on Perceived Value and Intention to Use
items.abstract: This study investigates the benefit–sacrifice trade-off of artificial intelligence (AI)-powered fashion services by examining how perceived benefits (usefulness, timeliness, enjoyment) and perceived sacrifices (technical effort, privacy risk, lack of personalization) shape consumers’ perceived value and intention to use, drawing on the Value-based Adoption Model (VAM). Survey data were collected from 420 Millennial and Generation Z (MZ) consumers with prior experience using online fashion platforms, and the measurement and structural models were evaluated using SPSS 25.0 and AMOS 25.0 through confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modeling, mediation analysis, and multi-group analysis. The results show that timeliness and enjoyment significantly increased perceived value, whereas usefulness and enjoyment directly increased intention to use. Technical effort negatively affected both perceived value and intention to use, while privacy risk showed no significant effect. Unexpectedly, lack of personalization positively influenced intention to use, suggesting that young consumers favor exposure to broad market trends over restrictive, narrowly tailored recommendations. Perceived value mediated the effects of the benefit–sacrifice factors, and consumer trust moderated the value–intention relationship, strengthening it among high-trust consumers. By integrating VAM with a benefit–sacrifice trade-off perspective, this study offers theoretical and practical insights for designing effective AI-driven fashion commerce strategies.

items.title: The Blurring of Reality in the Age of AI: Development of the AI-Induced Reality Perception Confusion Scale and Its Association with Generative AI Literacy and AI Anxiety
items.abstract: This study sought to develop the AI-induced Reality Perception Confusion Scale (AI-RPCS) and investigate the mediating role of AI-induced reality perception confusion in the association between GenAI literacy and AI anxiety. In Study I (N = 355), exploratory factor analysis revealed a single-factor structure, and item response theory indicated that the items displayed high discrimination and suitable difficulty. In Study II (N = 332), confirmatory factor analysis indicated satisfactory model fit indices for the single-factor structure. Significant relationships among the variables supported criterion validity. In Study III (N = 408), structural equation modelling indicated that AI-induced reality perception confusion mediated the association between GenAI literacy and AI anxiety. These results demonstrate the AI-RPCS's initial psychometric validity. Furthermore, this study suggests that GenAI literacy may be associated with lower levels of AI-induced reality perception confusion, which may, in turn, be associated with lower levels of AI anxiety.

items.title: The Changing Landscape of Video Production Through Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping video production by extending automation, prediction, and generative capabilities across pre-production, production, post-production, and distribution. This chapter synthesizes recent literature on generative video, animation, visual effects, workflow automation, human-AI collaboration, adoption, and responsible use. The evidence indicates that AI can reduce production time and selected costs, improve consistency, accelerate ideation, and broaden access to sophisticated production capabilities. These benefits, however, depend on technological maturity, workforce competence, organizational readiness, creative autonomy, and governance. Persistent concerns involving authorship, copyright, authenticity, labor displacement, bias, deepfakes, and audience trust complicate adoption. The chapter proposes an integrated framework that positions AI not as a substitute for human creativity, but as a production infrastructure that redistributes creative and technical work while requiring human oversight, accountability, and context-sensitive implementation.
